content: The study evaluated the effects of moderate-intensity, multicomponent balance exercise interventions lasting at least one year compared to non-exercise control groups. The results showed a significant reduction in the risk of becoming an injurious faller among participants in the exercise group compared to the control group. Three additional trials reported no cases of injurious falls in either group. The evidence was assessed as having no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. The analysis also examined the impact of exercise interventions on fall-related fractures. A significant reduction in the number of people experiencing fractures was observed in the exercise group compared to the control group. However, three trials reported no fractures in either group, and one trial was excluded due to low compliance with the intervention. The evidence for fall-related fractures was downgraded due to imprecision and potential publication bias. For older adults aged 60 years and older, the effects of various exercise interventions on the risk of falls or fall-related injuries were assessed. Resistance exercises and multicomponent interventions showed mixed results, with some studies reporting improvements in physical function, balance, and cardiorespiratory fitness, while others found no significant differences. Pilates training, lasting 4 to 24 weeks, was evaluated in three trials, showing no significant differences in physical performance measures compared to control groups. Similarly, fastand moderate-velocity resistance training showed no differences in functional capacity measures such as timed up-and-go tests, chair stand tests, and walking tests. Exercise interventions, including aerobic and resistance training, were also studied among older adults with sarcopenic obesity. These interventions, lasting 8 to 26 weeks, were associated with significant improvements in grip strength and gait speed. However, the evidence was downgraded due to serious risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision. Physical activity interventions among pre-frail and frail older adults (mean age 79–84 years) showed variable results. Some studies reported significant improvements in physical performance measures, such as gait speed, balance, and lower body strength, while others found no significant effects. Tai Chi interventions experienced high dropout rates, limiting the reliability of the results. Yoga interventions were evaluated in older adults (mean age 61–84 years) across 17 trials. The results were inconsistent, with some studies showing improvements in physical function compared to inactive controls, while others found no significant effects. The evidence was downgraded due to inconsistency, indirectness, and imprecision. Active video games were studied in older adults (mean age 76 years) to assess their effects on physical performance and balance. The results were inconsistent, with some trials showing improvements in timed up-and-go scores, while others found no significant effects. Measures of balance varied widely across studies, and the evidence was rated as very low quality due to imprecision and risk of bias. The association between physical activity and social support among older adults was examined in 27 studies. Most studies reported a positive association between physical activity levels and social support, while a few found no association or a negative relationship. The evidence was limited by reliance on self-reported physical activity and variability in the scales used to measure social support and loneliness. The review also updated the search for studies on fall prevention interventions, extending the search to November 2019. The data collection process involved independent reviewers screening and extracting data, with disagreements resolved through consensus. The primary outcome of interest was the rate of falls, and similar exercise interventions were grouped using a taxonomy developed by the Prevention of Falls Network Europe (ProFaNE).
